crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
children.blurb: The AI enablement audit is a structured review of whether an investment firm can actually use artificial intelligence safely, not just whether it has bought or built any.

children.name: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Fair lending and bias testing covers the review of credit decisions, pricing, underwriting and marketing for unlawful disparities by race, sex, age, national origin and other protected classes.

children.name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
children.blurb: Explaining models to regulators and clients is the practice of translating how a model was built, what data it used, and how it behaves into terms a non-specialist overseer can check.

children.name: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
children.blurb: Protecting material non-public information covers the handling of facts about a company that are not yet public and that a reasonable investor would consider important to a trading decision.

children.name: Verifying What a Model Produced
children.blurb: Verifying what a model produced means checking an output against something other than the model itself: the source documents, a calculation, a rule, or a second system.

sections.body: Governance and fiduciary risk covers the work of proving that an AI system used in finance behaves lawfully, fairly and accountably. In practice this means running enablement audits before tools are deployed, testing lending models for disparate impact, producing explanations that regulators and clients can follow, keeping material non-public information out of model prompts and training data, and checking that what a model produced is actually correct. The work is procedural and documentary: logs, test sets, approval records, review notes. It sits with compliance, risk and legal teams rather than with the engineers who build the models, though it depends on engineers to make the systems testable in the first place.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Bias testing and model documentation are the most mature parts, with established statistical methods for comparing outcomes across groups and standard templates for model cards and validation reports. Data loss prevention has decades of practice behind it, and the hard part now is that prompts and chat interfaces create new channels for sensitive text to leave an institution. Explaining a model to a regulator remains genuinely difficult for complex systems, and much of what passes for explanation is a plausible narrative rather than a faithful account of the model's reasoning. Verifying output is the least settled area, because a fluent answer can be wrong in ways that only domain review catches. The honest limit across all of it is that governance reviews are periodic while models and their inputs change continuously, so any approval is a snapshot.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from preparation to detection to explanation to protection to verification. The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms is the entry point, covering how a firm checks that a tool is fit for its intended use before it reaches production. Fair Lending and Bias Testing takes that further into credit decisions, where the concern is measurable differences in outcomes and the statistical work of finding them. Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients addresses the communication problem once a model is running and someone outside the team asks why it decided what it decided. Protecting Material Non-Public Information deals with the boundary around sensitive data, including the routes by which it can leak through prompts and vendor systems. Verifying What a Model Produced closes the loop on the output itself, asking how a person confirms that a generated answer, summary or figure is right before it is relied on. Read together they form a sequence a practitioner would follow, and each stands alone for someone who needs only that step.
